## The Problem 

Data in psychology:

- are often skewed

- do not respect normality assumptions 

- estimates are computed on small samples

::: {style="font-size: .7em;"}

Traditional tests such as the t-test and the anova are focused on means, but differences might arise in other parameters, such as skewness and kurtosis.

The overlapping index calculates the area of overlap between densities of the data and the overlapping test is based on permutation, therefore assumptions free.

The case in example applies the overlapping index on environmental data.

:::

## An extreme example


```{r esempio1, warning=FALSE,message=FALSE, cache=TRUE}

normPars <- c(10,2)
unifPars <- c(0,20)
n <- 30 

x <- rnorm(n, normPars[1], normPars[2])
y <- runif(n, unifPars[1], unifPars[2])

LIST<-list(x,y)

Y <- stack( data.frame(y1=x,y2=y) )

```

# Compute mean and standard error
summary_data <- Y %>%
  group_by(ind) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_value = mean(values),
    se = sd(values) / sqrt(n())
  )

# Plot bar graph with error bars
ggplot(summary_data, aes(x = ind, y = mean_value, fill = ind)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = position_dodge(), width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = mean_value - se, ymax = mean_value + se),
    width = 0.2,

  ) +

    x = "Groups",
    y = "Variable of interest"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +

   )

## The Overlapping Index 

::: {style="font-size: .9em;"}

The Overlapping Index ($\eta$) is an index of **effect size** and varies from 0 and 1. 

The Index calculates the area of overlap between two or more **groups/conditions**. 

It is computed on the density distribution of the data and it is normalized to 1 when there is complete overlap and when the distributions do not have points in common, meaning that the groups/conditions are disjoint, $\eta = 0$

:::


## Permutation test

::: {style="font-size: .8em;"}

Usually $H_0$ is defined as the absence of an effect.

For simplicity, instead of working with $\eta$ now we will work with the complement $\zeta$, defined as $1 - \eta = \zeta$ and define $H_0 : \zeta = 0$ meaning that there is no difference between the densities of the two populations.

The permitation test:

-   Rearranges the data $B$ times
-   Calculates the statistic for each new dataset of permuted data
-   Calculates $p$- value as the probability of obtaining equal or more extreme values


```{=tex}
\begin{eqnarray*}
p = \frac{(\# \hat{\zeta}_b \geq \hat{\zeta})+1 }{B+1}
\end{eqnarray*}
```

:::

# Application on real data

## The study {.smaller}

AIM -- Compare Outdoor and Indoor teachers on:

- Affective qualities of school places (School organizational climate - R-SLEQ)

- Life satisfaction (Satisfaction with life - SWLS)

- Psychological distress (Psychological distress - DASS-21)

Hypothesis -- Outdoor teachers report:

- More favorable organizational climate (R-SLEQ)

- No differences in life satisfaction (SWLS)

- No differences in psychological distress (DASS-21)

## Sample characteristics

```{r descriptive}
#| results: hide

Dati_insegnanti <- read_sav("data/Dati insegnanti10-2021_3.sav")
names_cols <- c("DASSTot", "RSLEQTot", "SWLS")
mean(Dati_insegnanti$DASSTot[Dati_insegnanti$OutIn == 1], na.rm = T)
mean(Dati_insegnanti$DASSTot[Dati_insegnanti$OutIn == 2], na.rm = T)
n_DASStot_in <- sum(!is.na(Dati_insegnanti$DASSTot[Dati_insegnanti$OutIn == 1]))
n_DASStot_out <- sum(!is.na(Dati_insegnanti$DASSTot[Dati_insegnanti$OutIn == 2]))

# n_RSLEQtot_in <- sum(!is.na(Dati_insegnanti$RSLEQTot[Dati_insegnanti$OutIn == 1]))
# n_RSLEQtot_out <- sum(!is.na(Dati_insegnanti$RSLEQTot[Dati_insegnanti$OutIn == 2]))
# 
# file.edit("data/Scale (1).sps")

```



- 136 Italian teachers (96.3\% women), mean age = 45.16 years ($SD = 10.64$, range $24-64$)
- 66.9\% primary, 31.6\% kindergarten, 1.5\% lower secondary school
- Outdoor teachers: n = `r n_DASStot_out`
- Indoor teachers: n = `r n_DASStot_in`


# Results R-SLEQ

## STEP 1:

**Data visualization and Descriptive statistics**

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
#| warning: false

library(overlapping)
RSLEQtot_in <- Dati_insegnanti$RSLEQTot[Dati_insegnanti$OutIn == 1]
RSLEQTtot_out <- Dati_insegnanti$RSLEQTot[Dati_insegnanti$OutIn == 2]
List_RSLEQ <- list(RSLEQtot_in, RSLEQTtot_out)

```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)


RSLEQ_data <- data.frame(
  Score = c(RSLEQtot_in, RSLEQTtot_out),
  Group = factor(
    c(
      rep("Indoor", length(RSLEQtot_in)),
      rep("Outdoor", length(RSLEQTtot_out))
    ),
    levels = c("Indoor", "Outdoor")
  )
)


ggplot(RSLEQ_data, aes(x = Score, fill = Group, colour = Group)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.25, linewidth = .5) +
  labs(
    x = "RSLEQ Total Score",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Group",
    colour = "Group"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 16),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )

```

## STEP 1: 

**Data visualization and Descriptive statistics**

\

```{r}

names(List_RSLEQ) <- c("Indoor", "Outdoor")


desc_table <- lapply(names(List_RSLEQ), function(group) {

  d <- psych::describe(List_RSLEQ[[group]])

  data.frame(
    Group = group,
    N = d$n,
    Mean = d$mean,
    SD = d$sd,
    Skewness = d$skew,
    Kurtosis = d$kurtosis
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows()


knitr::kable(
  desc_table,
  digits = 3,
  col.names = c("Group", "N", "Mean", "SD", "Skewness", "Kurtosis"),
)
```

\

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false

overlap(List_RSLEQ, plot = F)
```

## STEP 2:

**Significance Testing**



```{r}
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
perm.test(List_RSLEQ, paired = F, B = 1000, return.distribution = F)
```

```{r}
Zdist_RSLEQ<- perm.test(List_RSLEQ, paired = F, B = 1000, return.distribution = T)
Zobs_RSLEQ <- Zdist_RSLEQ$Zobs
Zpval_RSLEQ <- Zdist_RSLEQ$pval
```


```{r}
Zperm_RSLEQ <- as.vector(Zdist_RSLEQ$Zperm)
ZPERM_RSLEQ <- data.frame(Zperm_RSLEQ)

ggplot(ZPERM_RSLEQ, aes(Zperm_RSLEQ)) + 
    geom_vline(xintercept = Zobs_RSLEQ, lty=2) + 
    geom_density() + 
    xlab(expression(paste(hat(zeta), " distribution"))) + 
    ylab("")  +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 16),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 25)
  )
```


## STEP 3:

**Tailored parametric specific testing**

```{r}

model_RSLEQTot <- aov(RSLEQTot ~ OutIn, data = Dati_insegnanti)

```

One Way Anova: $F(1, 134) = 7.98$, $p = 0.006$

**Assumption of Normality Check**

```{r ttestRSLEQ}

Res_RSLEQTot <- model_RSLEQTot$residuals

ggplot(data.frame(Res_RSLEQTot = Res_RSLEQTot), aes(sample = Res_RSLEQTot)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#3a86d4", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 16),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16)
  )

```

## To Conclude

- No detectable difference in Life satisfaction 

- No detectable difference in Psychological Distress

- Outdoor teachers reported more positive affective qualities of school places

## Take home message

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="65%"}

-   Be aware of parametric tests assumptions

-   Always plot your data BEFORE running the analysis

-   Thinking Before Testing (cit. Richard McElreath )

## The Overlapping Index {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {style="font-size: 1em;"}

The Overlapping Index ($\eta$) is an index of effect size and varies from 0 and 1, formally defined in the following way:

```{=tex}
\begin{eqnarray}
\eta (A,B) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} min [f_A (x),f_B (x)] dx
\end{eqnarray}
```
$\eta (A,B)$ is normalized to one and when the distributions of A and B do not have points in common, meaning that $f_A (x)$ and $f_B (x)$ are disjoint, $\eta (A,B) = 0$

:::
